name: The Authorship Rule
title: The Authorship Rule
answer: The Authorship Rule is a school-wide agreement that students must make their own creative work and disclose any AI help they use. It matters because without a clear line, a student can submit an AI-generated image for an art assignment and honestly believe nothing was wrong. The rule protects both the integrity of creative subjects and the student's understanding of what authorship means.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: The Authorship Rule sets a single, simple expectation for creative subjects: the student makes the work, and any AI assistance is disclosed. It solves the confusion that arises when schools have no stated position, where a student might hand in an image generated in seconds and see no problem with it. The rule does not ban AI outright. It permits specific, limited uses such as brainstorming ideas for a painting, finding reference images, or learning about an artist's techniques. It also allows layout tools like Canva for Education or Adobe Express for Education, provided the artwork and design choices remain the student's own. What it forbids is presenting AI-made work as the student's own creation.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the rule is posted and shared with families using the format in Figure 10.3, so teachers and parents see the same standard. Creative assignments are marked at the lower AI use levels from Chapter 3, which keeps most day-to-day work clearly in student hands. A small number of assignments may explore AI directly, for example a project where a student compares their own drawing with one generated by AI and discusses the differences, and those are clearly labeled as such. The text does not separate this guidance by grade band, though it notes that the copyright discussion suits older students. The same rule applies across arts, music, physical education, and health work.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no research evidence for the rule itself, so it rests on practice rather than research. It does cite one external point: UNESCO's guidance notes that the United States Copyright Office has said output generated by AI is not protected by copyright, because copyright protects only work that comes from human creativity (Miao & Holmes, 2023). The book presents that as a teaching point for older students rather than as proof that the rule improves learning.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The rule draws its limits around authorship, not around technology. AI may support thinking, reference gathering, technique learning, and layout, but it may not stand in for the student's own creation. Disclosure is required whenever AI help is used, and any assignment that explores AI directly must be clearly labeled so it is not mistaken for ordinary creative work. The decisions about which uses are acceptable on a given assignment stay with the teacher, and the judgment about whether a piece is the student's own work stays with a person. The copyright point is included as a discussion topic, not as legal advice.
